title: DNS — The Phonebook of the Internet
description: Learn how DNS translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses through a hierarchical, cached resolution system.

segments.text: You type 'google.com' into your browser. But computers don't understand names — they need IP addresses. Something has to translate that name into a number. That something is DNS.

DNS isn't one giant lookup table. It's a hierarchy. At the top sit thirteen root name servers. Below them are TLD servers — dot-com, dot-org, dot-io. Below those are authoritative servers that know the actual IP addresses.

When you make a DNS query, your device asks a recursive resolver — usually your ISP's server. This resolver does all the heavy lifting, walking down the hierarchy on your behalf until it finds the answer.

The resolver uses iterative queries. It asks root: 'Where is google.com?' Root says: 'I don't know, but ask the dot-com TLD server.' The resolver asks TLD. TLD says: 'Ask Google's authoritative server.' Finally, it gets the IP.
That's a lot of round trips just to find one IP address. Four hops minimum. Seems expensive, right?
segments.thought_prompt: How could we avoid making all these round trips for every single DNS lookup?

segments.text: The answer is caching. Every step in the chain caches results. Your browser caches DNS. Your operating system caches DNS. The recursive resolver caches DNS. Most lookups never even leave your machine.

Each DNS record has a TTL — time to live. It tells caches how long to remember the answer. A TTL of three thousand six hundred means 'cache this for one hour.' After that, ask again. Short TTLs mean faster updates but more queries.

DNS doesn't just map names to IPs. A records point to IPv4 addresses. AAAA records point to IPv6. CNAME records are aliases. MX records route email. TXT records store arbitrary text, often used for verification.
Traditional DNS is sent in plaintext — anyone on the network can see what sites you're visiting. DNS over HTTPS encrypts those queries, wrapping them in the same secure tunnel your web traffic uses.
DNS over HTTPS is great for privacy. But it means your ISP can't filter malicious domains anymore. There's always a tradeoff.
segments.thought_prompt: Should DNS privacy override an ISP's ability to block malicious domains? What's the right balance?

segments.text: DNS is the internet's phonebook — hierarchical, cached, and surprisingly elegant. It resolves billions of queries per day with sub-millisecond responses, all because of smart caching and delegation. Next, we'll dive deep into HTTP itself.
